title: I can’t figure out why I don’t seem to like certain fast-paced action films

commenti.body: Watch some old Hong Kong action movies, such as hard boiled, or Dragons forever. They pretty much perfectly nailed how to do action movies, with crazy stunts, and well choreographed fight scenes. I’m not as huge on newer action movies either, not that they’re bad, just not my thing.

I'm not quite sure it makes sense to compare Rush Hour and Mad Max: Fury Road. Rush Hour has action sequences, but it's first and foremost a light-hearted buddy comedy. Mad Max: Fury Road, on the other hand, is non-stop, dystopian action movie with very little lightheartedness to speak of. I don't think they're in the same category at all. Having said that, both of them are good at being what they are, so it doesn't surprise me that you liked them both. Similarly, although I'm not the biggest John Wick fan in the world, it does what it sets out to do very well, so it's not a surprise that you like that one, too. 

I guess what I'm saying is that in any genre, not just fast-paced action, there are going to be well-done movies and poorly-done movies. Fury Road and John Wick are almost universally-beloved by action fans, while Hardcore Henry and Dredd are not. So yeah, I think you just like the movies you like because they're better.

I haven’t seen any of the films you mentioned not liking, but for me personally classic action is maybe the genre that is being negatively affected the most by the arrival of digital and CGI. The action just feels weightless. Fury Road strikes a great balance, but we’ll see what happens with the Furiosa prequel.

I'm a big fan of these types of movies (including the ones you say bored you), but the big difference I see between something like Fury Road or John Wick and The Raid/Dredd/HH is that the latter films lack pathos, especially The Raid and Hardcore Henry, which are borderline experimental in their complete and total disregard for plot. 

The Raid gives you a vague abstraction of stakes, with the pregnant wife and the offering of Salat that opens the film, but rest of the film's runtime is just insanely brutal choreography. Dredd is an anti-hero in the truest sense-- that film is, to crib DND terminology, about Lawful Vs. Chaotic evil, and doesn't give you much to root for outside of inventively filmed carnage for it's own sake. John Wick is definitely a student of The Raid, but Stahelski fleshes out his characters a lot more and creates a compelling and stylish world (I think Dredd does this too, but without any nagging dead wives or lovable puppies). IMO The Raid is a masterpiece of cinema, but I wouldn't begrudge anyone who found it dull, it's basically an hour long fight scene that takes place in several identical hallways and apartments. The Raid and Hardcore Henry are purist genre exercises that exist to satisfy freaks like me, who will watch every dogshit Scott Adkins/Dolph Lundgren direct-to-disc/streaming programmer that comes out because they love good fight choreography. Those films are beloved by genre fans because they do action so, so, so incredibly well, to the detriment of things like compelling storytelling or complex characters.

I think Dredd is a lot more well liked than Hardcore Henry. Not as much as John Wick, certainly, but that's probably one of the few films since The Matrix to really influence the action films that followed it.

The Raid and Dredd are both fairly dark (tone and visuals) action films. Dredd in particular is set in a dystopia, but it barely touches on it, it's all back drop.

I think having an affinity for that kind of bleak seeing possibly helps.

Have you seen the original RoboCop? That's somewhat similar to Dredd in terms of the world, but is much more of a satire
